title: Star and mesh topologies

stations.name: Star topology
facts: Every device in a star connects to the central switch, and all data passes through it.
Each device has its own dedicated cable to the switch. Cables to every other device would be a full mesh.

questions.q: What is at the centre of a star network?
questions.a: A switch

questions.q: How does each device connect in a star network?
questions.a: With its own cable to the central switch

stations.name: Advantages of star
facts: Each device has its own cable, so a cut cable only affects that one device. There is no other route, so the data can't be rerouted.
The switch forwards each piece of data only where it needs to go, which keeps traffic down.

questions.q: One cable in a star network is cut. What happens?
questions.a: Only the device on that cable loses its connection

questions.q: Why does a star network perform well?
questions.a: The switch sends data only to the device it is meant for, so there is less unnecessary traffic

stations.name: Disadvantages of star
facts: The switch is a single point of failure: everything depends on it.
Running a separate cable from every device to the switch adds up to a lot of cable and installation work.

questions.q: What is the biggest weakness of a star network?
questions.a: If the central switch fails, every device loses its connection

questions.q: Why can a star network be expensive to install?
questions.a: Every device needs its own cable back to the switch, which uses a lot of cable

stations.name: Joining star networks
facts: Linking the switches lets devices on one star reach devices on the other.
Each star still works on its own. Only traffic between the two stars is cut off.

questions.q: An office has two star networks, each with its own switch. How are they joined together?
questions.a: A cable links the two switches

questions.q: The link cable between the two switches is cut. What happens?
questions.a: Devices can still talk to others on the same switch, but not to devices on the other switch

stations.name: Break it!
facts: Only Sales 2 is cut off. Everyone else's cables and switches still work.
Everything plugged into Switch A loses its connection. Accounts and Conference are on Switch B with the server, so they are fine.
Accounts and Conference share Switch B with the server. Reception and Sales are stranded on Switch A.

questions.q: The cable between Sales 2 and Switch A is cut. Which devices can no longer reach the file server? Select all that apply.
questions.a: Sales 2

questions.q: Switch A fails. Which devices can no longer reach the file server? Select all that apply.
questions.a: Reception; Sales 1; Sales 2

questions.q: The link cable between the two switches is cut. Which devices can still reach the file server? Select all that apply.
questions.a: Accounts; Conference

questions.q: Which single failure would stop every device from reaching the file server?
questions.a: Switch B fails

stations.name: Full mesh
facts: In a full mesh every device has a direct link to every other device.
Each of the 4 devices links to the 3 others: 4 × 3 = 12, but each cable joins two devices, so 12 ÷ 2 = 6.

questions.q: What is a full mesh network?
questions.a: Every device is connected directly to every other device

questions.q: How many cables are needed to connect four devices in a full mesh?

stations.name: Mesh: pros and cons
facts: There are many routes between devices, so data simply takes a different one.
The number of cables grows quickly as devices are added, which makes a full mesh costly.

questions.q: One link in a mesh network fails. What happens?
questions.a: The data is rerouted along another path

questions.q: What is the main disadvantage of a full mesh network?
questions.a: It needs a lot of cable and is hard to set up, so it is expensive

stations.name: Partial mesh: the internet
facts: Routers connect to several others, which gives plenty of alternative routes without linking every pair.
Because the internet is a mesh, other routes are available around the failed router.

questions.q: Why is the internet a partial mesh rather than a full mesh?
questions.a: Connecting every router to every other router would need an impossible amount of cabling

questions.q: A router on the internet fails. What happens to data that was going to pass through it?
questions.a: It is sent a different way through other routers

stations.name: Wireless mesh
facts: WAPs pass data to each other by Wi-Fi, so each one needs at least one neighbour in range. Only one needs a cable.
Every hop between WAPs adds delay, and walls and other devices can weaken the signal.

questions.q: In a wireless mesh, what must be true of each wireless access point?
questions.a: It must be within range of at least one other WAP

questions.q: What is a disadvantage of a wireless mesh compared with a wired network?
questions.a: It can be slower and less reliable, because data hops between WAPs and walls cause interference

stations.name: Star vs mesh
facts: Use these to answer the worksheet question: why is a mesh network better than a star network, and when would you still choose a star?

questions.q: Sort each statement: does it describe a star or a mesh network?
questions.a: The central switch is a single point of failure = Star; Data can be rerouted if a link fails = Mesh; Uses the least cable of the two = Star; Each device connects to several others = Mesh; A new device needs just one cable to the switch = Star; The internet is an example = Mesh

common: Naming a term without saying what it does.
Giving an advantage with no reason attached.
Repeating the question in the answer.
